本组英文评阅原文: WorkOf gives design-conscious homeowners, collectors and design professionals a reason to explore: it connects independent-maker furniture with finished interior ideas. The Company page explains this positioning, while Work and Design separate product discovery from room inspiration. The restrained presentation supports the craft message. The Nordic Sled Chair detail page shows a photo carousel, a ¥499 price and options to save a favourite or open a wishlist. The Still Heaven design page also offers a project enquiry form with project-type choices and says visitors can expect a reply within two business days.

The product path still lacks details needed for a confident purchase. Work offers only three selected pieces, and the Nordic Sled Chair page shows photos and a price but no visible maker, materials, dimensions, availability or delivery terms. The buttons “Favourities” and “Wishlist” make the save action unclear, and “Favourities” is misspelled. A notice explains that a demo order is unpaid and has no delivery, which sets expectations but leaves shoppers without a clear way to confirm availability.

Add a short specification block to each product with its maker, materials, dimensions and availability, plus a clear contact route for delivery details. Replace the two save labels with one consistently named “Save to wishlist” action and explain what happens after it is selected. These changes would help visitors compare products and understand their next step, while keeping the design enquiry route for people seeking customised spaces.

YiPaiHe gives local pickleball players a convenient way to plan a visit. The homepage separates shared play, private-court bookings and ball-machine practice, with prices and links to check available times. The address and opening hours are also easy to find. This helps customers compare their options without repeatedly asking about prices and availability in a WeChat group.

In our test on 3 November, we could view the court schedule before logging in. The 16:00 shared session on Court 1 showed three remaining places at ¥25 per person. When we selected two players, the estimated price changed to ¥50. The page also distinguished available and full sessions. These details helped us check whether the time, group size and cost suited our plans before creating an account.

One detail that could be clearer is the playing time for late sessions. The homepage describes shared play as a three-hour session, but selecting 22:00 in our test gave only 30 minutes before the venue closed at 22:30, still at ¥30 per person. The booking notes explained the shorter duration, but someone choosing a session quickly could overlook this and expect more playing time.

We suggest showing a clear reminder when a late session is selected, such as “Only 30 minutes of play before closing at 22:30.” The actual playing time should appear beside the price before the customer continues. We also could not find clear cancellation or rescheduling rules on the public pages checked during the earlier review. A short explanation of these rules and the expected confirmation time would help customers decide whether to book.

RZL Studio has a clear focus on BNBU students who need headshots, everyday campus portraits or graduation photographs. The service descriptions explain what each option is suitable for, while the portfolio lets students see the photography style before making an enquiry. When we selected the Graduation filter, the portfolio changed from 24 works to six relevant photographs. This made it easier to focus on the type of session we were interested in.

The pricing details are useful for students planning their budget. The website lists separate charges for makeup, extra participants and additional retouched photographs. It also explains that the campus package includes five edited photographs for the whole session, rather than five for each person. The booking form states that refusing permission to use photographs in the portfolio will not affect the service. This gives students a clear choice about how their photographs may be used.

However, we found one confusing price example. The Pricing page lists a one-person indoor campus session with two extra retouched photographs at ¥150. When we entered these choices in the booking form, the estimate was ¥190, including ¥40 for the two extra photographs. A student using the example to plan their budget might expect the lower price and then be unsure which amount is correct.

We recommend correcting this example and checking the other examples against the booking calculator. It would also help to explain how soon customers can expect a reply and how long photo delivery normally takes. These details matter to students booking photographs for an application deadline or graduation. Including them near the enquiry form would help students decide whether the service fits their schedule.

Campus Food Map gives BNBU students, especially new and international students, a clear reason to use it. It brings dining locations, stall information and student ratings together on a bilingual map. Showing Chinese and English names side by side helps students who are still learning their way around campus match what they see on the map with signs on campus.

When we searched for “noodles”, we found relevant stalls across several canteens without having to know a stall name. The Shifang Food Court list also reordered its stalls when we selected “Score”. Showing how many ratings each score is based on helps students put the results in context, and the rating and feedback options give them a way to contribute.

The SVG map uses D3.js for panning and zooming and groups markers that would otherwise overlap. The search supports keyboard navigation and matches queries regardless of letter case or spacing. The JavaScript separates the map, search, detail panels and API requests into different modules. On smaller screens, the detail panel moves to the bottom so students can browse stall information while keeping part of the map in view.

The main gap is the information students need to decide whether to visit a stall. For example, the detail panels for Yu Zhanggui Bench Noodles and Yujian Noodles showed that prices, opening hours and photos were still to be added. We could find both stalls, but we could not tell whether they fit our budget or when to go.

We recommend starting with a small set of freshers’ picks and giving each one a food photo, a bilingual dish description, a price range and opening hours. That would make it easier for new students to choose a meal and plan a visit. Allowing page zoom would also help students who need to enlarge small text or map labels.

BNBU Drink Guide addresses a practical problem for international students who are unfamiliar with Chinese drink menus. It combines English descriptions, Chinese names, pinyin, prices and shop locations so students can choose a drink and prepare to order it in person. The Explore, Locations and How to Order pages support different steps of that decision.

On Explore, searching for “naicha” returned relevant milk tea options. In a separate test, we searched for “boba” and combined the Milk Tea, MissaIceCity and Under ¥12 filters. The only result was Brown Sugar Boba Milk, listed at ¥8. Its detail panel showed the Chinese name and pinyin, gave a short ordering tip and linked directly to the shop’s location in Building V25. The How to Order page explains sweetness, ice levels and useful phrases in Chinese, pinyin and English, giving students something they can refer to at the counter.

The JavaScript search supports English, Chinese and pinyin and handles variations in pinyin spacing and tone marks. The site stores filter choices in the URL so users can share or reopen the same results. The drink details use a native dialog that can be closed with Escape and returns keyboard focus to the original drink button. The card grid and navigation also adapt to smaller screens.

The main improvement is to clarify how prices relate to cup sizes. For example, Boba milk tea at A Little Tea is listed as “¥12 / ¥15”, but the detail panel does not say which size goes with which price. We recommend labelling each price with the corresponding size and showing any extra charges for toppings. A Chinese order card that combines the drink name, size, sweetness and ice level would also give students something they can show the cashier directly.

For mobile browsing, the site could store the exact image file path for each drink and load images farther down the page only when needed. The current code tries several file extensions before finding an available image, so using the exact path would avoid unnecessary requests.

FreeCoffee gives environmentally interested individuals, families, schools and coffee shops a clear reason to visit: it connects coffee-ground reuse with growing experiences and workshops. The homepage explains the reuse process and offers separate participation routes. When I selected “personal growing” and “simple experience” in the two-question recommender, it suggested the Family DIY Standard kit, explained the match and linked to the product and growing guide. This made the next step clear for a beginner.

The product information helps visitors evaluate suitability. The education filter returned one range clearly labelled “planned”; the family kit page listed a 750g specification, a ¥25 reference price, temperature guidance and daily watering requirements. These details helped me assess the space, effort and likely budget involved. The pages also distinguish concept images and planned kit contents from confirmed arrangements. Submitting an empty enquiry displayed four specific errors with links to the relevant fields, making correction straightforward. However, the form explicitly sends and stores nothing. The homepage names Xiaohongshu and WeChat channels without an obvious direct contact link, so I could explore the offer but could not use the enquiry form to reach the team.

Add a verified contact email, account identifier or scannable QR code beside each demonstration enquiry form, and clearly label it as the route for a real enquiry. For the family kit, confirm the available species, included accessories, delivery area and current price, while retaining the clear labels for planned products. These changes would reduce uncertainty and give interested visitors a practical way to turn their interest into a product enquiry or workshop discussion.
